speechtext:

should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has the Prime Minister any clarifying statement to make with regard to the letter from J. Edgar Hoover, director of the F.B.I., read to the United States security committee yesterday by Attorney General Brownell to the effect that comments were made regarding the appointment of Harry Dexter White to a position on the international monetary fund by sources highly placed in the Canadian government?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: STATES COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As I read the report I understood this was a letter from Mr. Hoover, and I knew nothing about the existence of such a letter until I saw the report in the newspapers. The matter has been discussed with my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), because I must confess I was quite surprised to see brought out in any inquiry before a committee of congress references to what must have been, if there was anything, confidential information communicated by a Canadian official to a United States official.
As soon as we saw the report, proceedings were immediately instituted to ascertain if there had been any such communication and how and when it had been made. So far we have not discovered anything that would enable us to trace any such communication. But the inquiries are continuing, and if and when we do find anything that would tend to confirm the report, or to put us in a position to make a positive denial, that information will be communicated to the house.

subtopic: RELEASE OF KOREAN PRISONERS OF WAR

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: RELEASE OF KOREAN PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Has the attention of the minister been drawn to a report of the speech by the United States Secretary of State in which he stated that
Korean prisoners of war would be released on January 22 whether or not a peace conference has been held? I would also ask if this is a decision of the United Nations, and if not was Canada consulted regarding it? In any event, what is Canada's position regarding the matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RELEASE OF KOREAN PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
The hon. member's
question seems to be threefold. The first part of it has reference to the statement that Mr. Dulles, the United States Secretary of State, made the day before yesterday, I believe, concerning the decision of the United Nations in respect of the disposition of prisoners of war in Korea. I assume that Mr. Dulles was speaking on behalf of the unified command under the United States, to which the United Nations security council by resolution on July 7, 1950, recommended that all United Nations members providing military forces for the Korean effort make such forces available. Therefore Mr. Dulles on this occasion was speaking on behalf of the unified command, that is the United States.
The second part of the question has to do with whether Canada was consulted about this statement. Canada was not consulted about this particular statement but the subject matter thereof is one on which there has been a frequent exchange of views in the past between the United States and other countries, including Canada, which have contributed forces to the United Nations command in Korea.
The third part of the question was: In any event what is Canada's position with regard to the matter of disposition of prisoners of war in Korea? I think that this matter is dealt with by paragraph 11 of the terms of reference for the repatriation commission as laid down in the armistice agreement. The provisions on this point are, I think, quite clear and mean, as we understand them, that if the Korean political conference does not meet before the expiration of the 120 days during which the prisoners are in the custody of the repatriation commission, or if the conference does meet within this period but fails to agree on the disposition of the prisoners within the time set, then the repatriation commission is obliged to declare the release of the prisoners in its custody from prisoner of war status to civilian status. That is the position as we understand it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxion (Minisier of National Defence):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REMOVAL TO MONTREAL
speechtext: My attention had not hitherto been drawn to this report, but assuming as I do that the report says what the hon. member has stated, I cannot give him assurance that it is erroneous because it would be quite correct. subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REMOVAL TO MONTREAL
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Why is it necessary to move this establishment from Esquimalt to Montreal?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REMOVAL TO MONTREAL
speechtext: We think it is very desirable to economize in matters of money and men. We have established a central supply depot at Ville LaSalle. It is to act as a supply depot for all Canada. It seems sensible to me to establish a school for supply officers and men at the central depot rather than to continue at Esquimalt, which is already overcrowded and where we need space for other naval requirements.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate I would like to extend my congratulations to you, sir, on the appointment that has been bestowed upon you. It is fortunate indeed that the house has a man of your experience and proven ability to assume that high office.
I would like also to congratulate the mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and the seconder (Mr. Vil-leneuve) of the speech from the throne. It seemed to me that they carried out their duties in the best tradition of parliamentary debates. I think the house should be happy about the large number of able young men
The Address-Right Hon. C. D. Howe that have joined us during the first session of this parliament.
The participants in this debate have spoken about several matters on which it would be appropriate for me to comment. On this occasion, however, I intend to confine my remarks to the grain situation in western Canada. At some later point of our proceedings I hope to be able to give my usual report on economic conditions and prospects throughout Canada but in view of the attention that has been paid to the western grain situation, I feel that hon. members will expect me to give priority to this particular subject.
I do so most willingly because it is important that the house and the country generally should have the facts about the current grain situation and should not be misled by the propaganda that has been spread abroad by those who are trying to discredit the wheat board method of handling grain or who are interested in making the outlook appear as black as possible.
To begin, let me state a few more or less obvious facts. First, the large stocks of wheat now on hand have not accumulated because the farmers of the prairie provinces planted excessive acreages to wheat. Look at the figures. The acreages sown to wheat in the past 2 or 3 years have been no larger than they were 20 years ago, in the early 1930's.
Second, the large stocks of wheat now on hand have not accumulated because sales have been low. Quite the contrary. Canada has never sold so much wheat so rapidly as during the two crop years which ended on July 31 of this year. Again look at the figures. Exports of wheat and wheat flour during the crop year 1951-1952 amounted to 356 million bushels and during the 1952-1953 crop year to 385 million bushels. An average year's export in the 10 pre-war years was 200 million bushels and in the 10 years immediately preceding 1951-1952 was 260 million bushels.
If wheat did not accumulate because of large plantings or deficient exports, then why did it accumulate? For one reason and one reason only-because of phenomenal yields. The 1952 crop was the largest ever grown on the prairies; the 1953 crop was the second largest and the 1951 crop was the fourth largest. Never before have two bumper crops followed one another. This is the third bumper crop in a row. Hon. members from western Canada know as well as I do that a normal crop is around 350 million bushels of wheat. Prior to 1951, the 21-year average was 329 million bushels. In 1951 the prairie farmers

The Address-Right Hon. C. D. Howe harvested 529 million bushels of wheat; in 1952, 664 million bushels; and in 1953, 584 million bushels, a total in those three years of 1,777 million bushels. To put it another way: five ordinary crops have been harvested in three years.
Mr. Cold well:	Is the minister using the
most recent figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes. I corrected the figure as a result of the report of the bureau of statistics made yesterday. The figure published yesterday was the wheat production for all of Canada. This is the latest figure for the prairie provinces.
That is the reason and the only reason for the present accumulation of wheat. It is not excessive acreage or poor sales. The reason is phenomenally good weather, which I for one cannot look upon as a calamity, nor does any western farmer, I am perfectly sure.
The fact is that if only average crops had been grown on the prairies during the past three years, we would not have been able to satisfy the world demand for Canadian wheat, there would have been no carryover whatever into the present crop year, and our supplies now would be barely adequate to meet the current demands. I am sure every thinking person is glad that nature was good to us, that we did have wheat to supply to a hungry world and that today we have a good supply to carry forward into years when nature may not be so kind.
I believe every thinking person will be glad too that during this period of large crops there has been a Canadian wheat board with the responsibility for marketing those crops. As hon. members know I am not a strong advocate of government in business. On the whole, I lean in the other direction. But from experience I have become convinced that the present system of grain marketing whereby farmers market their wheat, oats and barley through the Canadian wheat board has been very much in the interests of the producers.
Perhaps under some other government, perhaps with a different membership on the wheat board, the results would have been less satisfactory. All I know is that the present wheat board, operating under the general supervision of the present government, has disposed of vast quantities of grain at good prices and that, surely, can be accepted as a measure of its success.
The Canadian wheat board is directed by parliament to sell grain acquired by it-and I quote from the act-"at such prices as it considers reasonable with the object of promoting the sale of grain produced in
fMr. Howe (Port Arthur).]
Canada on world markets". The board has, in my judgment, carried out that direction fully and with a great measure of success. Under the present government it will continue to do so.
Hon. members will recall how the wheat board and the government were criticized for selling wheat at what some people considered were prices lower than could have been obtained. I seem to remember that some hon. members on the other side joined in that kind of criticism. Now the board and the government are being criticized for the opposite reason, that prices are being held too high.
A few weeks ago I spoke to the annual meeting of the Manitoba wheat pool in Winnipeg about such criticisms and should like to repeat here what I said at that time.
To be criticized for keeping prices down, when such criticism is unjustified, is annoying. But it doesn't do any harm to sales of Canadian wheat and flour. In fact the board used to welcome this kind of criticism. It made good reading in overseas markets. To be criticized for holding prices higher than they should be, when such criticism is unjustified, is quite another thing. It can serve no purpose other than to influence buyers to avoid forward commitments, in the hope that prices will eventually be lower.
The buyers of wheat the world over know the facts of the current wheat situation at least as well as they are known in Canada. They can be depended upon to buy shrewdly, and it is to be expected that they will emphasize the bearish aspects of the situation. They don't need the help of people in Canada who, it would seem, are more concerned to discredit the present system of wheat board operation than they are to assist in the disposal of Canadian wheat.
There has never been any reason to accuse the Canadian wheat board of holding prices at levels which endanger the sale of Canadian grain. And there is no justification for such accusations now. From long experience, the members of the board know that such a policy leads to disaster. As long as I have anything to do with it, the board will follow a pricing policy which keeps the buyer interested in Canadian grain.
So much by way of general introduction to the present situation. As a result of the phenomenal crop of recent years, and in spite of record sales, there was a large carryover of grain into the present crop season. It could not have been otherwise. Physically, we couldn't have moved into consumption all the grain that farmers wished to deliver from the extraordinary crops of 1951 and 1952. If, as might well have happened, the prairies, in 1953, had suffered the calamity of a drought, or an early and severe frost, this carryover would have been of the very greatest immediate value.
Instead, however, there was another ideal growing season and a bumper crop on the prairies. Unfortunately, the harvesting of yet another bumper crop coincided with a

decline in the immediate import requirements of several of our chief markets, due to good domestic crops and large stocks. This was an unfortunate coincidence but it is one that could not have been foreseen or provided against.
Even so, grain has been moving off the farms, into terminal positions and for export at a pretty fair rate. To judge from some of the comments I have heard in recent weeks, one might get the impression that the grain movement had come to a stop. Nothing could be farther from the truth. In some respects the movement is at record levels.
Let me deal with exports first.
Compared with the past two years, when new records were established, the export movement of wheat is down. But the reduction to date is far less than some people seem to suggest. From August 1 to November 4, which is the latest date for which figures are available, export clearances of wheat and flour amounted to 80-7 million bushels as against 103-7 million bushels to the same date a year ago. As for barley and oats, total exports are running well ahead of last year, which was itself a record year for exports of both these grains. The total for the three grains is down only 19 million bushels from the same period in 1952-53.
It might interest those hon. members who are not already aware of the fact that a new record was established this year for clearances of grain from Churchill. On the Pacific coast, grain is continuing to move out at close to the maximum handling capacity of the ports. The effect of the reduction in export demand has been concentrated entirely at St. Lawrence ports.
I am pleased to be able to report to the house that Canadian wheat and flour is moving steadily into the United Kingdom, which has always been, and I hope always will be, Canada's biggest market for wheat and wheat products. Now that the business of importing wheat and flour into the United Kingdom has been restored to the private trade, purchases are being made from day to day in relatively small quantities to meet the needs of individual mills, just as they were made in pre-war years. The situation is complicated, too, by the fact that the government of the United Kingdom is turning its larger than normal stocks over to the private trade. There are no longer large bulk contracts, but these individual purchases add up, and I hope that before the end of the crop year the United Kingdom will have bought very substantial quantities from Canada.
The Address-Right Hon. C. D. Howe
I have heard it said that Britain's failure to enter the international wheat agreement is hampering the sale of Canadian wheat to the United Kingdom. It seems that the Leader of the Opposition shares this opinion. In view of the biased and often quite erroneous information that has been given out about the international wheat agreement, I am not surprised that some people should jump to such wrong conclusions, or should try to create wrong impressions. Let me say again, as I have said in this house before, that wheat agreement or no wheat agreement, Canadian wheat will be fully competitive on the British market. It is fully competitive now, and there is no reason to believe that British mills will buy less from Canada than they would otherwise buy because the United Kingdom is not a member of the international wheat agreement. We are certainly getting a fair share of the British market now. I believe we are getting as large a share as in any peacetime year and perhaps a larger share.
During the last parliament I gave a clear statement of the views of the government about the international wheat agreement. We believe that it is in the interests of all countries, importers and exporters alike, to be members of the agreement, so as to reduce excessive fluctuations in markets and prices for wheat. We were disappointed when the United Kingdom stood alone in not accepting a renewal of the agreement. I would point out to the Leader of the Opposition that the United Kingdom did not declare its position until the final moments of the conference when practically all other countries, including all the main importers, had agreed to a floor price of $1.55 and a ceiling of $2.05. That is why the U.K. decision came as such a disappointment, not only to Canada but to every other country represented at the conference. It was not Canada that rejected the U.K. offer; it was the U.K. that rejected the overwhelming view of the rest of the wheat world. In our judgment, this was an unfortunate decision for all concerned, including the United Kingdom.
During the discussion that followed the signing of the agreement, there was a good deal of talk that the United Kingdom had not signed because it could not agree to a price of $2.05. It was pointed out at the time that this was only a ceiling price, that prices could, and might well, fall below that level. In fact prices have fallen below $2.05 from time to time, and this would have been the case whether or not the United Kingdom had joined the agreement.

The Address-Right Hon. C. D. Howe
However, this is threshing old straw. There is an international wheat agreement. The United Kingdom is not at present a member. Nevertheless we are selling wheat and flour to the United Kingdom, and I see no reason why we should not continue to do so in large volume. Certainly the Canadian wheat board will spare no effort to perpetuate the mutually profitable wheat trade that has been built up between Canada and Britain. I hope some day the United Kingdom will rejoin the club, but that is a decision that rests with the United Kingdom government.
The wheat board is out selling Canadian grain whenever and wherever it can. Mr. McNamara, the assistant chief commissioner, has just returned from several weeks in the United Kingdom and on the continent of Europe, calling on customers for Canadian grain. He has reported to me that, in his opinion, Canada will continue to get a fair share of the grain business in that part of the world. He found that Canadian grain stands high with the buyers in comparison with wheat from any other country. Mr. Riddel will leave at the beginning of the year for a tour of markets in the Far East and' possibly in other parts of the world, taking with him Dr. Anderson, the chief chemist of the board of grain commissioners, and Mr. Vogel from my department. Other officials of the board have recently been visiting markets in Latin America.
The board knows that it has a tough job on its hands. But I am confident, and I think most hon. members are confident, that the job could not be in better hands. A few days ago Mr. Earle Robertson was added as the fourth member of the wheat board. Mr. Robertson was highly recommended to me by men in the co-operative grain handling organizations whose judgment I trust as a man exceptionally well qualified to help in marketing Canada's grain. I was delighted when he accepted the appointment.
While I am talking about the export side of the grain business, may I add a word about the deferred pricing system which seems to have been misunderstood in some quarters.
Until recently, when a buyer came in to purchase wheat from the board-or book wheat, as it is called-he paid the board's announced price in effect on that date of booking-even if actual shipment of the wheat did not take place for some months. Some overseas buyers have claimed that this could be too long a period' to be carrying wheat at a fixed price. So the board set up a deferred pricing system, in addition to its former fixed price system. Now, when a


buyer books wheat with the board, he can fix the price on the date of the booking or, if preferred, he can defer the pricing for a specified number of days. Within that period the buyer can choose the day on which he wants his wheat to be priced, but his choice is of course not retroactive. If the price on the day of his choice is lower than it was on the day he booked the wheat, then he has gained by deferring the price fixing. But, on the other hand, of course, if the price is higher on the later day, the board and the producers benefit. It is definitely not a case of "heads I win, tails you lose". If the price is down, the buyer profits. If the price is up, the producer profits. The system is working very well and certainly has facilitated the export sales of our wheat and flour. Since in the last analysis most of the buyers are millers the chief merit of the system is that it enables the millers to fix the price of their raw material on a date as close as possible to the time when it will actually be processed.

speechtext: Will the minister tell us for how long a period the decision can be deferred?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I believe it is seven days from the date of shipment from Montreal, and fifteen days from Vancouver.
Now let us look iat the internal movement of grain.
Receipts of prairie grain at the Pacific coast between August 1 and November 4 of this year totalled 40-5 million bushels. This compares with 35 * 6 million bushels in the same period a year ago. Lakehead receipts totalled 136-8 million bushels of grain as against 149-6 million bushels a year ago. Shipments out of the lakehead by boat to November 4 totalled 128-2 million bushels, 4-2 million bushels more than in the same period of the crop year 1952-53.
I would like at this point to pay tribute to all those who have contributed to the achievement of this large internal movement which has been of the greatest value in creating space in country elevators to enable prairie farmers to market their grain.
Now I come to the point that I know is of direct and immediate interest to hon. members from the prairie provinces, namely the ability of producers to market their grain. When the present crop season opened on August 1, there were 215 million bushels of grain in country elevators as against 154 million bushels on August 1, 1952. Thus, in spite of the large movement eastward and westward, there was bound to be less opportunity for producers to deliver grain at

the beginning of the season than there was a year ago. And yet I do not think the figures by any means support some of the gloomy statements I have seen and heard about the delivery position.
As a matter of fact, up to November 4 producers had delivered 207 million bushels of grain and the latest information of space likely to be available suggests that deliveries between August 1 and December 31 will exceed 300 million bushels and could reach 325 millions. This is a respectable total and more than has been delivered during this part of the season in many previous years.
The Canadian wheat board established an opening delivery quota of three bushels per cultivated acre. Because last year's opening quotas were five bushels for wheat and four bushels for each oats and barley, there is an impression in some quarters that last year's quotas were larger. That is not correct, because last year's quotas were per seeded acre and did not take summerfallow into account. In point of fact, this year's quotas are very little different from last year's, considering the average amount of summerf allow a farmer will normally have.
It has already been possible to increase the minimum quotas that may be delivered within the over-all quota of three bushels per cultivated acre from 500 bushels to 700 bushels and it is my hope that before very long the over-all quota itself can be increased.
Because of the limitations on delivery opportunities the government has been urged to provide for advances on farm-stored grain. Let me assure the house that even before these representations were received the government had given the most careful consideration to the position.
We decided that the quickest way of getting a large sum of money into the hands of western producers without putting them into debt was to speed up the payment of participation on the 1952 crop. This we did. A further interim payment of 12 cents per bushel was declared on 1952-53 deliveries of wheat.
The 1952-53 pools of oats and barley were closed out. Altogether these payments involve about $100 million. Already cheques valued at $72 million have been mailed to producers and the balance of the $100 million will be in the mail before Christmas.
The Address-Right Hon. C. D. Howe
Having declared their payments, the government had a look at the income of prairie grain producers in recent years. As hon. members are aware, there has been a big change in the pattern of deliveries in recent years. Up until a few years ago farmers delivered most of their grain soon after harvest. As a result of the more than average crops and particularly as a result of the exceptional crops of 1951 and 1952, this pattern has changed. Producers have been delivering grain steadily and in very large quantities throughout the whole year.
Now let me outline the results of the calculations of income of prairie producers derived from the principal grains-wheat, oats and barley. I shall begin with the calendar year 1945. In that year, prices paid at time of delivery basis Fort William-Port Arthur plus participation payments by the wheat board, amounted to $537 million. In 1946 the amount was similar, $536 million, in 1947, $588 million, in 1948, $693 million, in 1949 because of large participation payments on the five-year pool, $833 million and in
1950,	$605 million.
Now I come to the first of the three successive phenomenal crops, the crop grown in
1951.	During the whole of that calendar year prices paid plus participation payments jumped to $898 million. In the following year, 1952-that is, last year-they reached $1,091 million.
When I spoke to the Manitoba pool on October 27, I hazarded a guess that the income figure for 1953 would exceed 1951, which was itself a year of very good income, but might fall a little short of 1952. I now find that I erred on the side of pessimism.
I hate to be on that side. The fact is that the sum of prices paid for deliveries of wheat, oats and barley plus participation payments during 1953 will exceed 1952. Making conservative estimates for November and December, the total is placed at $1,104 million, which exceeds any previous year. These payments do not include the final wheat participation payment for the 1952 crop, which will be paid early in 1954, and which in total amount should be substantial.
With the permission of the house I should like to put a table on the record giving the figures I have just mentioned.

Mr. Speaker, I very much welcome the opportunity of speaking at an early date in this debate, particularly after just listening to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and his statement on the wheat situation in Canada.
I intend to refer at some length to what I think is a very serious and critical situation facing western farmers, particularly in the marketing of western wheat, and I take exception to the perennial optimism expressed in the minister's speech as delivered to the house just now.
I consider it, Mr. Speaker, to be a very great honour to be returned to the House of Commons to work with my colleagues, the members of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation. I intend to do my utmost to promote the objectives of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation because, upon returning after some absence from this house, I feel that the policies of the C.C.F. are the only ones that can bring sanity to the financial and economic problems facing Canada. Upon returning to the house I was rather impressed with the isolationist attitude and feeling one gets in parliament here at Ottawa. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that if we could go across the country before coming into this house to debate problems before us and perhaps see some of the difficulties that exist from coast to coast there would be an urgency in our deliberations which would bring more action than we see at the present time.

The Address-Mr. E. G. McCullough
All is not well with the ship of state, despite what is indicated in the throne speech. I am sure that if we went from coast to coast and saw the problems facing Canadian people in the various sections of our country we would recognize that the whole Canadian economy is in a very serious situation. I am sure that would be so if we could experience the situation of the unemployed in the coal mines of Nova Scotia, the situation facing fishermen in the marketing of their fish, and the situation facing western farmers who have again produced food in abundance for Canadian people and a hungry world. If we could see some of those situations face to face in such a way that when coming into this house they would be fresh in our memory, I am sure we would go beyond the measures and legislation provided by the Liberal government.
This afternoon I wish to speak for three main purposes. First, I wish to bring to the attention of the house the desperate situation facing western farmers in regard to marketing and also the price squeeze in which we find ourselves; second, I wish to suggest proposals for rectifying that situation; and third, I wish to say something in a general way about our national economy.
Now, in comparison to the optimistic statement delivered to the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the western farmer is in a price squeeze. We have seen, particularly during the last two years, costs of farm operations going up and up while the prices received by the farmer for the things he has to sell are going down. Contrary to the statement contained in the telegram from Mr. Marler, president of the Alberta federation of agriculture, to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, which the minister read in the house, and which statement indicated that no serious marketing problem exists in western Canada, I want to indicate by documenting my speech that a very serious situation does exist.
Just before coming here I travelled pretty well throughout my constituency, which is representative of Saskatchewan. The local merchants have extended credit to the limit of their resources. In many parts of Saskatchewan local merchants, storekeepers and machinery dealers have held meetings and as a result thereof have gone on a strictly cash basis simply because they have taken the brunt of the lackadaisical attitude of the federal government and its lack of policy in coming to grips with the marketing situation in the west. To a large extent they are bearing the brunt of the situation that has been created.


So far as the carrying on of the work of the local municipalities is concerned, taxes are not being paid to the municipalities simply because the farmers are not able to sell their grain and pay their taxes. As a result there is a debt situation on the local level which is making it very difficult for local governments to carry on and for municipal councils to provide the necessary services. That is a very important thing in any community.
I should like to deal with the quota system existing in western Canada which will indicate to some extent that there is no money in the farmers' pockets. The three-bushel quota and the maximum of 700 bushels to any farmer do not give the farmer adequate money to pay his running expenses and his taxes.

I accept what the minister has said but I want to indicate to the house how it works out in practice. While I, and I think all members of this group, favour a quota system operating under the wheat board, it is and can only be an expedient. When you cannot deliver your grain, as has been the case at many points in Saskatchewan, whether it is a three-bushel quota or a maximum of 700 bushels does not mean very much to the farmer if he cannot get his grain to the elevator. Here is the situation as it works out in practice. There may be an opening in a certain elevator and word goes out that there is an opportunity to market some wheat. Perhaps there is only a maximum of a carload of wheat. Any farmer who wants to take advantage of his quota must deliver his wheat in order to get some money to carry on. If his wheat happens to be high-grade wheat and other farmers delivering to meet the quota and fill the space in the elevator have lower-grade wheat, then the farmer with the high-grade wheat must take a downgrading on his wheat and lose money on it. Many farmers are in that position and have to take a lower grade for their wheat in order to market it.
Then of course there is the car order book system which was discontinued temporarily bringing about an injustice to farmers, in my opinion, who wanted to market their grain through the elevator of their choice. I am glad to note that Mr. Milner indicated to the wheat board on November 9 that as soon as possible there will be a return to the policy of

the -car order book. 1 want to deal with one other aspect of the financial situation facing western farmers and -then to document my speech by indicating from various sources that what I have said presents the true picture rather than the rosy one painted -by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
With regard to cattle markets, I agree with the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny), who spoke yesterday in this debate. He indicated that because of the financial situation existing in western Canada farmers were shipping cattle -to the stockyards, and that there was no- adequate system of grading whereby they could be assured of -receiving a just grade for the -cattle they ship. That -is true, Mr. Speaker. That situation does exist. Just before -coming here for the -session I was -talking with a shipper -who had sent a carload of cattle to Winnipeg. One white cow was downgraded or knocked down two cents a pound simply because it was a white cow. I have also talked with shippers who have told me that in shipping cattle to Winnipeg animals which are a cross -between Herefords and Shorthorns, having mottled white faces, are also downgraded. In other words, simply because it is a buyers' market the buyers now have it in their hands to enforce a discount of two or three cents a pound and disregard the quality of the beef.

In his speech the hon. member for Dauphin indicated -that we should have a livestock board with adequate producer representation. It would be a beginning in giving some justice in the -marketing of our cattle. When you consider that cattle prices reached a high of 32 cents a poun-d you can -see that there was a fluctuation of about 50 per cent from the high to the low in the five-year period.
With respect to hog prices, there was a fluctuation of $10.77 per hundred in the year 1951. A market situation of this kind can only mean that the western farm producer is in a very difficult position to -plan his operations or to be able to carry on in a proper manner financially. Coming -back to the question of documenting the very serious situation that I have indicated, I first want to take the figure of loans made to western farmers -for the year 83276-9J

There were in that year 83,315 loans made totalling $98,259,152. Now, that is one example which shows that the western farmer has to go out and borrow in order to carry on. This is a very good act passed by parliament making it possible for farmers to get loans for farm improvements. These loans of course are made to farmers who need short-term and intermediate credit for the improvement and development of their farms and- the improvement of their living conditions thereon.
I should like to refer to the Globe and Mail. I think reference was made to this in the speech made today in the house by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). This excerpt from the Toronto Globe and Mail dated Thursday, November 5, indicates that the implement dealers are concerned about the situation also. This is what it says:
In a wire to Howe signed both by the Canadian federation of farm equipment dealers and the Manitoba and lakehead farm equipment retail dealers' association, delegates said: serious damage would- result to the national economy unless something were done to get farmers out of debt.
"We believe action by the federal government is required in both the interests of agriculture and industry," the wire said.
So, there is some concern among the dealers. As a matter of fact I was talking to a local dealer who had one of the head men come down to see him and he was concerned about their dealers all over the province not being able to get an extension of credit on the matter of retail sales of farm machinery.
I should like also to indicate the increase in the credit buying of our people because the farm situation and that of the people throughout the country are perhaps synonymous, and there is a parallel existing all across the country.
This covers the period from April to June of this year and the figures are taken from the dominion bureau of statistics. They report that on retail consumer credit notes record cash and credit sales amounted to $3,135,900,000. Total credit sales jumped 7-5 per cent to $1,020,400,000 compared with the same period last year, while cash sales rose only 4-1 per cent to $2,115,500,000.
Mr. Speaker, I indicated- earlier that the dealers are concerned about the matter of giving credit to our western people. This is a report of a meeting held by merchants in the city of Dauphin and it indicates that the estimated total debt of Canadians to storekeepers has reached a record of $1-5 billion and that this was 50 per cent more than at the end of March, 1952.

The Address-Mr. E. G. McCullough
In regard to the loans which have been made to Canadian farmers under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, it is stated, in the biennial progress and program report to the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations, that loans made during 1952 were $98,359,151 representing an increase of about 11 per cent over the previous year. Ninety-five per cent of the loans have been used to finance farm machinery purchased. The prairie provinces have made the most use of the loans, with 46 per cent of all farmers in Alberta receiving loans during the 21 months beginning January 1, 1951.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to the briefs tendered to the royal commission sitting at Regina in which it was indicated that two of the main reasons for the difficulties and problems facing rural dwellers is the instability of farm income. I think I have indicated an abundance of evidence to show that the western farmer today in particular is facing a very serious financial problem.
The speech which the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has just given to the house was substantially the same as his address to the annual meeting of the Manitoba wheat pool in Winnipeg on Tuesday, October 27.
1 I want to take exception to what he said there. First of all, he said that he did not believe the federal government should go into the business of lending money to the farmer. I agree with the proposition put forward by the leader of this group, for I believe it is expedient in the present situation that loans should be made to farmers so that they can pay their debts and carry on their operations. I do not think that such a policy is a good long-term policy, but I have a suggestion to make to this house further on in the course of my remarks.
The minister indicated today that the kind of speech which I am making, stressing the importance of something being done now, would make good reading for the importers of Canadian wheat overseas.
I think that the policy or lack of policy of the Canadian government in failing to take a hand in this problem or to do something of a substantial nature about it is the best kind of news the importers can get, because in spite of what the minister said, approximately 800 million bushels of wheat will be carried over into the next crop year. I do not think, in spite of what the minister said in the last part of his speech, where he indicated that he was pessimistic, that the picture needs to be a gloomy one. I should like to refer to the minister's speech to the wheat pool in Winnipeg, when he said:
I wonder if the Egyptians complained about a glut during the seven fat years predicted by Joseph.

We have heard much about this capitalist system, which is supposed to function in the interests of the people. I know full well, upon reading the record of the situation to which the minister has referred, that grain was stored in the good years for the bad or lean ones; and I am suggesting to the house today that in order to come to grips with this situation we have to be very realistic.
As is indicated in Toronto Globe and Mail of today, we will have a harvest this year of 613,965,000 bushels. That is about 20 million bushels over the previous estimate. I do not believe the minister or anyone else can predict how much wheat we are going to grow in the future. I do not think it can be said that we have now reached a time when we are growing an excessive amount of wheat; but I do feel that we should be glad of the large volume of that commodity in Canada today. It should be used as a bulwark against any future depression or crop failure in Canada. Every effort should be made to avoid cutting down but to increase possible production. We should try to get every acre into some sort of crop. I believe, too, that the federal government should subsidize the supplying of fertilizer so that increased yields would be possible. If this were done, there is a real chance that, rather than return to the smaller yields we had formerly, we might expect to have the high yields we have had in the last few years.
If this policy were undertaken we would have in Canada a large amount of wheat to stand as the best possible safeguard against any eventuality. I suggest that as a long-term policy we should establish in Canada the principle of the ever-normal granary. First of all, under this program the Canadian government should declare that it is proposing to establish the principle of the ever-normal granary. Under such a plan the target should be that within five years permanent storage facilities would be made available for a thousand million bushels of grain.
Then, third, under such a plan outright purchases of grain from the farmers should be financed from the federal treasury. Fourth, such a plan should begin immediately, as supplies of grain would warrant, and storage facilities should be provided to meet the requirements.
The first result of such a policy would be that it would have the effect of declaring to the world that there would be no fire sale of grain either now or in the future. Secondly, it would begin immediately to solve the problem of storage facilities. Third, it would give stability to all the Canadian economy by supplying farmers with purchasing power.

Then, fourth, it would provide an incentive to our primary producers to increase production. Fifth, it would give Canada the assurance that we could meet any commitments in connection with the export of our grain.
In his speech to the Winnipeg wheat pool the minister indicated that formerly there were times when we were in the position where we could not meet our commitments abroad for the export of our wheat. If we want to enter into any long-term agreement we should have wheat stored in Canada so that, under any circumstances, we could meet our commitments. I believe the method followed today, where we do not store under the ever-normal granary principle, indicates that we have in this country a hat-in-hand policy in the marketing of our grain. Instead of this we should have a program such as I have indicated.
I offer this idea in all sincerity. As an ambassador of good will and something to create friendship abroad, I am convinced that food will always be more effective than guns or, indeed, anything else. I am suggesting that a large amount of money be set aside to begin the program I have proposed. Despite the fact that the minister does not believe in a policy of making provision for storage facilities for our huge grain surplus, I believe the policy I have outlined would be accepted as good business. Those storage facilities should be made available immediately.
In the constituency of Moose Mountain we have large coal fields in which we strip the coal to a depth of about 45 feet. By using some engineering ingenuity, these huge excavations could be put to use in connection with the storage of grain. They could be cemented and lined with vapour-proof materials, and in this way make available at a low cost space for the storage of a huge amount of Canadian grain.
We are living in an atomic age, and do not know what events may bring at any time. I would hope that the proposals I have made would be undertaken by the government. I am aware of the fact that any capitalist government in this House of Commons always replies that these things would take a lot of money. My reply is that in this instance we should have an application of the principle that has been set forth by the government when it has said that what is physically possible should be made financially possible. If this principle were followed, the procedure I have outlined could be undertaken, and it would mean that we would embark upon a program under which the

I know that today one can drive anywhere in Saskatchewan and find wheat lying out in the open, wheat being destroyed by rain and by rodents. Surely this is a contradiction of the fundamental principles in which we believe. I am suggesting therefore to the government that it should undertake seriously a plan to store wheat in Canada for any eventuality, and for a long period of time if necessary-wheat perhaps to the extent of a thousand million bushels. I read in an Ottawa paper the other day a statement to the effect that stations were to be set up in the vicinity of Ottawa to observe flying saucers. Surely. they would not come down to what seems to me to be a type of insanity existing under the capitalist system. Therefore, Mr. Speaker,

We first met as freshmen at the University of Toronto in the fall of 1921, in a class which also included the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). It included later Mr. Russell Boucher, former member for Carleton; and that group added to their number on leaving university and entering Osgoode Hall law school in the fall of 1925 the hon. gentleman who is now the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), and the late Senator Joseph Bench. While there are in this new House of Commons 75 members who have not previously been members, there is, it is true, no great change in the balance, or should I more properly say the imbalance, that exists in the house. this I do not wish to detract anything from the victory which the government has won or that any hon. member has won. The fact of the matter is that scores and scores of hon. members in this house, and not least of all those who are among the supporters of the government, are here on a minority vote. I do not think we need spend very much time upon the speech from the throne. If it contains the legislative program of the government for the present session it is a very thin, puny program. It is evident that the session will be very short if that is all the government has to lay before the house in the way of a legislative program. The revision of the Bank Act will take some time and there will be extended discussion on some of the changes in the Criminal Code, but the balance of the program as adumbrated in the speech from the throne is impressive neither in content nor in length.
The amendment introduced by my leader two days ago puts before the house an opportunity to declare something that urgently needs to be declared in this country; that is, our profound belief that the welfare of Canada is dependent upon free competition and, second, that the prosperity and security of all Canadians will be advanced by government policies which will restore markets for primary products and generally promote a high volume of international trade.
Perhaps we should not be surprised that the leader of the C.C.F. took issue with our proposal that the house should declare itself in favour of free competition. We do not hear much of the C.C.F. Regina manifesto, but if the Regina manifesto still has a place among the policies and affections of the socialist members of this house then certainly they are still dedicated to replacing the capitalist system and to the establishment of a planned socialistic economy which will control finance and socialize -the insurance companies and many other matters which can never be squared with the assertion of our belief in the principle of free competition.
The second part of the C.C.F. subamendment proposes a plan of health insurance. It

This must cause no little embarrassment to some hon. members who support this government, one in particular being my good friend the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). Mr. Croll said he was sure the Prime Minister, with his deep understanding of human needs, would make a start on health insurance at the first session of the new parliament.

Health insurance will be introduced ''in due
course and by a Liberal government", Trade Minister Howe told a Liberal nominating convention here tonight.

A year ago the government thought the extension of the Emergency Powers Act for another year was sufficiently important to merit mention in the speech from the throne, but if the government has any such proposal in mind for this session it is certainly hiding its intention.
It will be recalled that this afternoon I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) a question which was naturally prompted by the complete silence of the speech from the throne on this subject. I asked whether it was the intention of the government to propose at this session the extension of that infamous measure which will expire on May 31 next unless renewed. If the government has made up its mind on this subject it should have the courage to come and tell us, because surely this is the time in the session and the speech from the throne is the means by which the house should be told what measures the government proposes to lay before the house at this session. This measure was important enough a year ago to receive special mention. Let the government now tell this house in all frankness whether it is going to bring in a measure this year to extend the infamous Emergency Powers Act. If that is its intention there should be early debate upon the matter and it should have had prominent mention in the speech from the throne.
I have time to make only one reference to the policies of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and to draw to the attention of the house the fact that during the contribution to this debate by the mover of the resolution, on November 13, the Minister of Finance made what may well prove to be a revealing comment. The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth), as recorded at the bottom of page 14 of Hansard, said:
This is another financial measure which will be introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) who, after bringing in seven budget surpluses in
(Mr. Fleming.]

the last few years, is probably looking forward to another.
The Minister of Finance then said:
Hear, hear.
It is quite evident, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance is completely unrepentant and that he is aiming again for another of these budget surpluses, the product of overtaxation. The budget surplus for the first six months of this fiscal year stands at $200 million.-another invitation to the government to indulge in more reckless spending.
Mr. Speaker, the subject of housing will, I hope, have a place of its own in debate at a later stage in this session. I comment on it now only to draw attention to the fact that it is absolutely inevitable and essential that something be done. The annual report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation under the National Housing Act, issued last summer, drew attention to the fact that the average income of those buying houses under the National Housing Act in the year 1952 was $89 per week. The average buyer paid $10,934 for his house, or 7 per cent more than he did in 1951. The income of the class of people buying houses under the act, we are told, rose even more dramatically than the price of houses. It jumped from $4,076 or approximately $78 a week in 1951 to $4,618 or approximately $89 a week in 1952.
The situation obviously calls for redress. We have been urging this for a long time in the house, and we shall examine with some degree of care whatever legislation the government introduces at this session to meet the needs of the situation.
I cannot leave this passing reference to the subject of housing, Mr. Speaker, without recalling the way in which one member of this house manages to get houses built in his constituency. I refer, of course, to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Speaking at his own nominating convention in the riding of Port Arthur last July, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said he had been told by people in his constituency that there was a shortage of mortgage money for the construction of houses in his riding. He then said this, and it is a direct quotation: "I instructed our treasury to make money available."
How many members of this house-yes, and at that time how many candidates for election to parliament-were privileged to the extent of being able to give orders to the national treasury that mortgage money be made available to his constituency? Is this the even hand of justice? Is this fair play to all constituencies? Or is this the old story of the Minister of Trade and Commerce

ensuring favours for himself and his constituency at a time when the extension of those favours would help to get him re-elected to this house? Mr. Speaker, housing is a national problem that affects all parts of this country, and there should be no favours extended to one particular part which are denied to other parts. I hope that hon. Liberal members of this house will not let this kind of discrimination pass without severe strictures against the man who perpetrated it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I draw attention to the fact that the opening reference in the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition sounds the note that the welfare of this country depends on free competition. That is our belief in this party. It is a timely assertion- timely because while some hon. members opposite have been giving lip service to the system of free enterprise their practices have fallen far short of the words. There was, for instance, the utterance of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in Ottawa on October 28, when he said the federal government does not intend to perpetuate monopolies in Canadian air line operation. Brave words indeed! But what are the facts? ... by their fruits ye shall know them.
They are a better test than their words. One calls to mind other words of Scripture:
This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.
The principle of free enterprise might well make that complaint against hon. members opposite.
I have not forgotten how, in participating in debate at McGill University with the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) a year ago, I heard him say this-and he was then a minister of this government: "The present Liberal government at Ottawa is neither free enterprise nor socialist". Those were his words. Then he went on to say: "The government of this country is a 50 per cent partner in every business enterprise in the country". Of course he alluded to the extortionate rates of taxation imposed by his colleague, the Minister of Finance.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, they say they are not socialist. If they are not free enterprise either, then what are they?

-in order to carry on a lawful enterprise in this country which has been asked for by no fewer than thirty boards of trade in the western provinces and offers great benefits and facilities to many shippers in this country, is of a piece with the paternalistic attitude exhibited by the government in the past in such matters as television, in restraining all forms of television in Canada until a matter of a year and a half or two years ago. That is the reason Canada was denied television for so long, the same old paternalistic attitude on the part of the government. They were not doing anything themselves and they would not let anybody else do anything, even to risk his own money in introducing a new business under the most proper safeguards.
Before I leave the subject of television I wish to make a comment on something that happened very shortly after prorogation of the last session of the house. We left here on the 14th of May. About ten days later a change in the allocation of television channels in the Toronto area was announced. Previously Toronto had had assigned to it under long-standing international agreements channels 6, 9 and 11. Channel No. 9 had been occupied by the C.B.C. for station CBLT. Sentiment had been running strongly, as every Liberal member from the Toronto area knows, in favour of putting these other channels to use. There were people ready to occupy them. But what happened? After getting parliament out of the way the government, through the Department of Transport, shunted channel No. 11 to an entirely different area.
When I got wind of the fact that such a proposal was coming before the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation I communicated with the senior Liberal member from the Toronto area, my good friend from Spadina (Mr. Croll). I sent him a copy of a letter I wrote to the board

of governors of the C.B.C. protesting against this proposal and urged him, and through him the other Liberal members in the Toronto area, to make their opposition to this transfer known to the board of governors. Whether any of them raised his voice or wielded a pen or pushed the key of a typewriter in opposition to this transfer I do not know. But nothing has been put forward publicly to indicate that any Liberal member from the Toronto area made the slightest effort to prevent that channel being taken from that area.
I do not take a narrow view with regard to the matter of assignment of channels. I wish to be fair in my approach to it. I have always approached my duties in this house, not simply on a local, but on a national basis. But I do wish to say that to deprive that area of a channel that had been recognized for years as one that belonged to it, iand which people in the area were clamouring that it should not only be retained but occupied, is but another example on the part of the government of how it is prepared to go on overlooking the needs of the central Ontario region.
The whole central Ontario region is deprived of any representation in the cabinet, notwithstanding the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), as long ago as June, 1949, when seeking support in the city of Toronto for the election of Liberal candidates in that area, promised that the area would receive representation in the cabinet. Here we are in 1953 and there is still no representation of that central Ontario area in the cabinet. It is not for lack of experienced and capable men. But the area is still denied representation. Is it not about time some hon. members of the house who come from that area, and who give their allegiance to the government, had something to say to the Prime Minister and to the government on that subject? Do not mumble it. Do not say it in whispers. Come out and say it openly as it ought to toe said.
There is little time left to discuss the vitally important subject of trade. In the year 1952 Canada stood third among the trading nations of the world, with external trade amounting to $581 per capita of population, exceeded only by New Zealand. But in the first nine months of this year for which figures are available a trend which is fraught with danger, a trend the dangers of which we drew to the attention of the house in the last parliament, continues. Figures for the first nine months of this fiscal year already show in a disturbing fashion that we are continuing to an increasing degree to put all our trading eggs in one basket, the

United States basket. These figures for the first nine months of this fiscal year show that 60 per cent of our total exports went to the United States and 73 per cent of all the imports which Canada purchased came from the United States.
Of our total trade, both export and import, 67 per cent or just over two-thirds was done with the United States. These figures are higher than they were previously. They show why we had occasion to warn the government about the dangerous extent to which our trading eggs are being put in one basket. I am glad that in a speech last spring the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) used the same expression, namely "putting our trading eggs in one basket". The danger is there, and it is becoming more and not less pronounced.
We are glad to trade with the United States, but we do not wish to run the risk of seeing such an overwhelming percentage of our trade being done with one nation. It is fraught with danger as anyone well remembers who recalls the lessons of 1921 and 1929, not to go back farther, with respect to our trade relations with the United States. On the other hand, there is that market in the United Kingdom which the government has so lightheartedly watched being curtailed. In the first nine months of this fiscal year only 16 per cent of our exports went to the United Kingdom, and we bought only 10 per cent of our imports from the United Kingdom.
We did not hear a word today from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) about measures the government has in mind for encouraging the expansion of our trade with the United Kingdom. On the contrary, Britain's purchases from us have been declining in the first nine months of this fiscal year. It is a serious decline, and today Britain's purchases from Canada are virtually confined to wheat and flour. That situation is fraught with peril for Canada. How much longer must we wait for some statement from the government, some adumbration of policy on the part of the government for extending our trade with the United Kingdom? Silence reigns on that subject.
We must purchase arms. What is the government doing by way of seeking to expand the proportion of those arms that we purchase from the United Kingdom? We had something to say about this subject last spring in the house, but to date we have heard nothing from the government as to efforts to expand purchases from the United Kingdom and in that way to provide Britain with needed dollars in order that she may 83276-10i
The Address-Mr. Fleming purchase wheat and other products which we would be glad to sell to her.
There are many other matters in connection with trade about which I had hoped to speak, but as my time is limited I pass now to one concluding subject which I lay before the government in no partisan sense. Canada, as we have been reminded in the discussion today and on previous days during this session, has been blessed by Providence with the second largest wheat crop in all her history. That has been a blessing in one sense, but at the same time it has created very serious problems when we measure the unprecedented carryover of wheat, a carryover that was measured by the dominion bureau of statistics a few days ago in terms of visible wheat supplies of 957 million bushels.
Mr. Speaker, there are areas in the world today where people are hungry. Mr. Trygve Lie, former secretary general of the United Nations, speaking in Cleveland a few days ago warned the world, particularly the western or free world, of this when he said:
There is no fact in the world, in terms of humanity and in terms of politics, which is more important than this: The vast majority of the people of the world live in poverty and misery and they know it and they don't like it. Most human beings are hungry today most of the time; more than half the people in the world are illiterate; half of the world's population is constantly ill, and expected to die before the age of thirty-five.
The communists know that and of course in areas like that they are seeking to mislead the people.
Now, there are nations within the commonwealth, and one thinks particularly of the Asiatic members of the commonwealth like India, Pakistan and Ceylon, where people are hungry today, where we are told people are starving today. Mr. Speaker, they look at reports of this huge wheat crop of ours, this huge surplus of wheat, and I am sure there are many questions that are in their minds, questions that are being exploited by the communists who never lose an opportunity of exploitation in such circumstances.
The government has received a number of memorials and resolutions on this subject. One of these came from the annual meeting of the executive council of the Church of England in Canada held last September. They put their resolution, after a number of recitals, in these words:
-petition the dominion government to make available to the hungry nations of the world, with the least possible delay, and, if necessary, at no cost, a tenth of this year's wheat crop.
I think the idea back of that was that it would be appropriate for Canada under conditions existing today to consider tithing her

The Address-Mr. Fleming bumper wheat crop to help to feed the hungry in the world. Mr. Speaker, I cannot speak of any particular quantity, which would depend of course on an examination of this problem. There are many factors involved in that, an investigation of the need, an investigation of the availability of shipping, and other factors which I am sure are quite obvious. But, Mr. Speaker, I urge that serious consideration be given to this need, particularly at a vital time like this when the communists lose no chance of exploiting every source of unrest and suffering in the world, and that we lose no opportunity to do something effective and if possible something dramatic, something that will catch the imagination of the world, particularly of the east, in a matter of this kind. Would it not be a major factor in showing the hungry people in the east today that we are with them, that our freedom expresses itself in a sympathetic and brotherly attitude, particularly to citizens of our sister nations within the commonwealth?
We should go forward and say "We are going to help you; we are going to help to feed you, and we are going to do it in a way that will strike the imagination of the eastern world, we hope of the entire world." The United States is giving shipments of wheat to these countries today. I will not try to put before the government any hard and fast or cast-iron proposal in this matter but I do urge, Mr. Speaker, that at a time like this when the eyes of hungry millions are directed towards Canada we may lose one of the great-i est opportunities that destiny has given to Canada if we fail to strike what will in effect be a great blow for freedom, as well as an act of great humanitarian and brotherly assistance to the citizens of our sister nations of the commonwealth.
We spend great sums on national defence. Here is one way in which an effective sum can be used in a way that may, far beyond the comprehension of any of us, help meet the challenge which is threatening openly in many parts of the world today. As the late Archbishop Temple, the Archbishop of Canterbury, pointed out, what force does when successfully applied in defence of freedom is simply to repel counterforce. It gives an opportunity for those who are willing to use it to create good will and those conditions which may make a repetition of a contest in arms not inevitable.
Mr. Speaker, here is a great opportunity for Canada to do something effective and something dramatic to fill the vacuum that has been left in the wake of force. We must have strength. No one in this house, I am
IMr. Fleming.]
sure, questions the necessity for our being strong, but this is not enough. Here is an opportunity given to Canada. Let us grasp it and be grateful for it.
